title: From Office Blocks to Boutique Apartments: How He Built a Whole Business Around Shanghai's Old Buildings
excerpt: Shanghai's urban renewal has thrown up plenty of opportunities, and the rapid rise of Yicheng Creative is just one snapshot of it.
body:
Shanghai's urban renewal has thrown up plenty of opportunities, and the rapid rise of Yicheng Creative is just one snapshot of it.

Shanghai's old districts are full of lanes. The lane off Shiziwan Road was once no different from the rest: a few office buildings standing beside a residential block and the residents' garbage heaps. But a little over three years ago, the designer Borja Trujillo Rodríguez turned a glove factory here into two pure-white buildings joined by a black "skybridge" — offices on one side, design apartments on the other.

"It was outrageous. It was like… an LV bag coming out of a slum." Shen Minkai still gets excited when he talks about the Shiziwan renovation. The project belongs to Yicheng Creative, the company he co-founded. Its main business is leasing old buildings on long terms, redesigning and renovating them, and then subletting them as offices or homes. With the Shiziwan project, Shen Minkai set out to create a brand called base, and Borja Trujillo Rodríguez built the black "skybridge" between the two buildings with the "base" logo on it.

Renovating old houses and old districts is an ever hotter subject in Shanghai. On Yongkang Road, 4 kilometers from Shiziwan Road, a street of wet-market stalls had by the summer of 2009 already begun turning into a "scenic neighborhood," with independent shops and bars squeezing in.

All these renovations can be seen as part of "urban renewal." Large-scale rebuilding first took place in 18th- and 19th-century London and New York. City managers wondered how to make their cities look more vibrant; residents often hesitated, worried that whatever replaced the old would be in poor taste; and real estate developers saw a chance to renovate existing stock (in plain terms, properties already in use and not for sale) and raise its value.

Shen Minkai is one such developer. By May 2015, Yicheng's base brand had 12 properties in operation (most of them in Shanghai), including the office space base Office, the serviced apartments base Living and the co-working space base Co, with a hotel, design services and a commuting business in the works. The style is simple and clean and keeps the raw, natural side of the materials. It is not especially daring, but it meets people's idea of "design," and the average occupancy rate is 88%.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703151729yNEx2FBi5ID1odac.jpg-w600)

![base Co. Image source: Yicheng Creative](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031517297RVUBLDryIGh1PnY.jpg-w600)

## **1.**

Shen Minkai started out as a lawyer. He graduated from Tongji University Law School with a master's degree in 2005 and went on to handle legal work in the real estate industry. In those years money poured in and out of real estate. Many of the cases Shen Minkai worked on himself involved broken funding chains and executives walking off with their loans. He concluded that real estate had become a market purely for big capital, where the richer the company, the better its chances. "So what are the small ones (companies) supposed to do?"

Some of them were converting old factories. Conversions need less capital than development, but they call for finer-grained management of leasing and operations. Shen Minkai believed this was the future. "Back then no one talked about 'existing assets,' but I felt there would definitely be a lot of them one day. As times change, you can't tear down and rebuild every building (in the city's core). Knocking everything down before it has served its use — that's impossible," he said.

The "existing assets" Shen Minkai refers to are not all old properties. They also include buildings of very little use value, which owners are glad to lease to specialist leasing operators to raise their value. "Look at how the developed countries of Europe and America have gone down this road over several hundred years, and I thought this was a pretty good industry," he said.

Looking back, his prediction was right. According to [a report by the real estate fund Gaohe Capital and the Policy Research Center of the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development](http://www.gohighfund.com/articles/article/945), by 2013 the first-tier cities of Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen had entered the "era of existing housing": most property transactions involved existing stock, new commercial property in city cores was very limited, and second- and third-tier cities were heading the same way.

Another trend also pushed Shen Minkai to start a business: rising demand for long-term rental apartments. In the first half of the 2000s, budget hotel chains leased large amounts of property in core business districts. Home Inns, for example, opened [26](http://finance.sina.com.cn/money/bwmx/20070723/06183809520.shtml) hotels between June 2002 and the end of 2004, and grew to [134](http://finance.sina.com.cn/money/bwmx/20070723/06183809520.shtml) between 2005 and the end of 2006. But Shen Minkai believed Shanghai already had enough budget hotels, while demand for rentals from white-collar workers, young people and migrants kept growing. These people rented rooms in ordinary homes, with "no feeling of home, no feeling of community, nowhere to interact" — and all of that was an opportunity.

In 2008, Shen Minkai teamed up with Shi Wei, an architect he knew well, to found Yicheng Investment Development Co., Ltd. in Shanghai, the predecessor of Yicheng Creative. With Shi Wei's family background in architecture and Shen Minkai's knowledge of real estate, moving into leasing and operating property looked like a natural step.

At first the company worked much like most others of its kind. It leased old buildings on terms of 5 to 20 years; the owners were usually the government and state-owned enterprises, which generally let or sold property through agreements and tenders. Design and architecture teams then reworked the projects, with construction and fit-out contracted to builders. After that came finding tenants and providing them with property management.

The "long-term rental apartment" plan, however, did not happen right away. Yicheng's early projects were in fact mostly "creative industry parks." Such projects had begun to appear in 2000. A well-known example is the Bridge 8 creative park on Jianguo Zhong Road in Shanghai, converted from the Shanghai Automobile Brake Factory, which went on to draw many design, creative, communications and consulting firms. Yicheng's projects were similar. Factory buildings, Shen Minkai explained, were better suited to conversion into offices, and cheaper to convert.

Yet in its first three years, Yicheng "didn't make money" from what looked like a proven business model. From the very first project, Shen Minkai found that "this stuff is really exhausting, and not that much fun." The projects depended heavily on access to property: get hold of an old factory, and the job was half done. Very little of the work involved "creativity." What gave him headaches instead were the many moving parts of running a project — licensing approvals, handover standards, permitted uses of the property, and the process and timeline for finding tenants all had to be thought through.

Money was no small problem either. A single project could easily cost tens of millions of yuan, and at one point Yicheng had to hand a project over to its partner Jinhe Commercial. "This business isn't as simple as being a sublandlord. Someone will say, I rent it in for 1 yuan and rent it out for 2, so I make 1 yuan. Sounds simple, right? But first you have to spend that 1 yuan. Then how do you rent it out for 2 yuan? Do you rent it out for one year or two? How do you turn something that cost 1 yuan into something worth 2? Those are all problems," Shen Minkai said. To this day, he tells people who want to get into the business to think twice.

In 2011, Yicheng briefly thought about quitting.

![The early project Yongjiating before and after renovation. Image source: Yicheng Creative; [Arting365](http://opus.arting365.com/entironment/2013-05-08/1367995450d270691.html)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703151730MpAvgI21QP6rk4e7.jpg-w600)

## **2.**

Two projects finished the next year, on Gaolan Road and Shiziwan Road, kept Yicheng in the business. Shen Minkai and his team also realized that design could create value, and so they created the base brand.

The Gaolan Road project was a small building of under 2,000 square meters, the former home of the Republic-era entrepreneur Yu Qiaqing. The old house had changed hands several times: before Yicheng's renovation it was a hotel; afterward it became an office building for BMW China. Because the project was small, it had to be done with more care. Yicheng hired Borja Trujillo Rodríguez, then a freelance architect, to design it.

Unlike the open-plan creative parks of the past, this renovation had a clear goal: to turn the building into modern corporate offices. The designer kept the original structure but stripped away the clutter, so that the cramped space better met clients' practical needs for an office. In the end the five-story building held not only offices but also an R&D center, a restaurant and a rooftop garden.

After the project was finished, Shen Minkai said, the team began to understand that the key to "design creating value" was "thinking from the client's side": what the market lacked most, which groups of people it was made up of, and which kind of building suited which kind of business. They "had learned how, and got going."

Borja Trujillo Rodríguez then went on to renovate another set of serviced offices and apartments on Shiziwan Road — the Shiziwan project described at the start. The architect worked "like playing with building blocks: knock out one piece, take down another, and build it back up." After the renovation, two long, narrow buildings of completely different styles became offices on one side and design apartments on the other. The offices were spacious and open, while the apartments offered a wide range of layouts and architectural details.

The interior design kept the original concrete and terrazzo and used reclaimed wood for the floors, to bring out the raw texture of the old building. At the same time, it added simple wooden furniture and soft furnishings, keeping the overall look fresh and understated.

![Before and after the Shiziwan Road renovation](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703151730dpYigX2OSzeFnMWJ.jpg-w600)

![The bridge between the two buildings bears the base logo; most of Yicheng's later projects feature this logo](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703151731rl2K4aVzey8SRhEm.jpg-w600)

![Interior design of base Living on Shiziwan Road. Image source: Yicheng Creative](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703151731Fk8U2WgJPTrM65q0.jpg-w600)

The renovation was impressive, but so was the cost. When it was finished in 2012, the best-equipped three-bedroom apartments in the best nearby compounds rented for no more than 7,000 yuan, yet Yicheng had to rent its one-bedroom duplexes for more than 10,000 yuan just to break even. Shen Minkai asked the designer to think about cost from the tenant's point of view: "You don't even earn 20,000 a month now. Would you pay 10,000 to rent this room? The foreigner was very sincere. He said, I really would. I said, on the strength of that, let's do it."

So the team studied many high-end serviced apartments and put a lot of thought into everything from furnishing the units and setting up sales channels to preparing the launch. When the project was finished and went on the market, the lowest price was set at 15,000 yuan a unit, with fairly attentive property management. A German rented the first unit for 15,500 yuan; the second went for 18,000. To the team's delight, all 13 apartments were let within six months. The tenants, like the designer, were mostly foreigners living in Shanghai.

This was the first project under Yicheng's base brand, and it set the design style for all of base's later projects: spaces kept "raw," "unprocessed" and "plain." Rodríguez also regards this renovation as his proudest work. He is now lead architect of Yicheng's in-house design team and a core member of the company.

Yicheng's in-house design team now has 6 foreign designers. The name base came from its Indonesian designer Lyla Charmaine Sulaiman, whom Yicheng hired as director of visual identity (VI) design.

Sulaiman believes the name base captures the opportunity in the Chinese market. After many years in China, she has grown tired, both visually and spiritually, of the luxury, the "maximalism" and the "more is better" attitude here. Like sharp observers in every field of design, she felt it was time to get back to basics and choose minimalism.

Shen Minkai has no strong feel for this, but he knows that if you want ever better buildings, you have to build your own brand. Since the Shiziwan Road project, Yicheng's properties have rented for noticeably more than comparable products from other companies, and much of the reason is the extra value of the base brand: "We can charge more of a premium, so we can afford to pay more to acquire a project, and I'm also willing to spend more on it." In base apartments, the towels, toothpaste, toothbrushes and soap all carry base's signature touch; the promotional brochures are made to look like newspapers and magazines, in packaging that matches the brand's style.

From 2012 to 2014, Yicheng renovated properties at several other sites in Shanghai, including Wulumuqi Road, Jianguo Road, Fuxing Road and Tianyaoqiao Road. Its clients included car companies, fashion companies, advertising, technology and design firms, and many employees of foreign companies and foreigners living in Shanghai. The ones you may have heard of are Grains, the busy cafe on Shanghai's Wukang Road, and Rachel's, the burger joint next door.

![Grains, a well-known cafe on Shanghai's Wukang Road. Yicheng did both the building renovation and the interior design. Image source: Yicheng Creative; [ShanghaiWOW](http://www.shanghaiwow.com/2015/08/4282)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031517321bkxMDhaOFBUzqec.jpg-w600)

## 3.

In early 2015, something happened that made Shen Minkai start thinking seriously about the company's strategy. Until then, he had believed that as long as he stuck to the goal of "do every project well once you land it, and make it look like base," the company would grow. But the founder of a well-known investment group asked him a few questions that struck him at the time as "strange": "Can what you make compare with our offices right now?" "Why are you able to rent it out?" "Where's your way in, and how do you show what your company is worth?"

Shen Minkai sat in the investor's office — a traditional office building with a traditional office fit-out — and could not answer. Investors were paying more and more attention to leasing and operating the existing assets that urban renewal had brought to market. Since 2013, long-term rental apartment chains in first-tier cities such as YOU+, MOFANG Apartments and Xinpai Apartments had raised money one after another. Long-term rental apartments were exactly what Shen Minkai had in mind when he first entered the industry.

Two months later, he seemed to find in that original idea the answer the investor wanted: start with people, and "fence the people in." A building's use can switch at any time among retail, commercial, office and residential, which means a property company must always be ready to respond quickly — no easy task. Shen Minkai believed that turning to holding on to users would be more effective.

"So I stopped thinking about buildings. I thought, only once I have people does my space have more use value. So whose business should I be after? Think about the base brand: I'm expensive, so how do I grab my own group of target customers and get them to build this platform for me? If I start with a base of ten thousand people, how much can I make? With a hundred thousand, a million, ten million, a hundred million — that would be huge," Shen Minkai said.

In its press releases, Yicheng describes its target customers as "creative nomads." Seeking a new way of life, expecting something from life and refusing to just work nine to five and go home — that is the "creative" part; not staying put in one place, living a life full of change — that is the "nomad" part. A more precise description comes from Yicheng's public share transfer prospectus: "middle-class and above value users with many things in common (such as being part of the floating population, highly educated, loving life, and on a middle to high income)." What makes them most valuable is that they "won't quibble over a difference of one or two thousand."

To that end, Yicheng widened the base brand's business, trying to make it look like a "closed loop" that could keep customers for the long haul. Besides serviced offices and long-term rental apartments, base's products include the co-working space base Co, which stresses socializing; the short-distance transport service base Go, still in planning; the resort hotel base Escape; and the design service base Décor. On some weekends and holidays, Yicheng holds a market called Weekend Collective. The magazines and books, jams, jewelry, New Year goods, artworks and other items on sale there all come from Yicheng's tenants, clients and the followers of its WeChat official account, who are invited to the market for base-style "community exchange."

It is hard to tell whether any of this really works, but the sales figures do say something. In an interview with QDaily in January 2016, Yicheng's operations director Cai Qi said that rents at base's residential project "Tianyao Xincun" ranged from 15,000 to 30,000 yuan, and that within three and a half months "almost all of it has been rented out." The later *Recommendation Report* from the brokerage that sponsored Yicheng's listing (note: this is a short name for the report; click to see the [full document](http://pdf.dfcfw.com/pdf/H2_AN201512180012194236_1.pdf)) cited the project's quick leasing as a key reason Yicheng turned a profit in 2015.

![The market held at base Co on Anfu Road before the 2016 Spring Festival. Image source: base's official WeChat account](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703151732kX6h0mseSZA2PrLC.jpg-w600)

## **4.**

The problem came back to money.

Shen Minkai planned to list Yicheng on the NEEQ (the "New Third Board"), which would help the company raise funds more easily. Yicheng now looks like a mature company when it comes to renovation and leasing, but companies like it always hit funding problems in the up-front development stage. Most of Yicheng's lease contracts with owners run for 8 years or more, a sizable one-off investment, while rent comes back in installments over a long period. As a result, Yicheng lost money in both 2013 and 2014.

In the *Recommendation Report* submitted in September 2015, the sponsor, Guangzhou Securities, said that Yicheng had entered the industry early, had a brand advantage and a fairly stable customer base, but it also warned investors of several risks: 90% of Yicheng's revenue comes from rental income that is slow to recover; Yicheng does not own the properties it leases, and suppliers could take them back at any time; and more competitors doing the same kind of renovation have appeared.

By the end of 2015, these problems seemed partly solved. Yicheng raised a Series A round led by Warburg Pincus, a US private equity firm that specializes in consumer goods, industry, technology, financial services and energy, and that has done quite a few real estate deals in China.

According to Shen Minkai, over the next two to three years Yicheng will join Warburg Pincus in buying existing properties. Yicheng will co-invest 10% in every project Warburg Pincus takes part in, and the projects will carry the base name. Yicheng will also move into brand management and licensing, offering a full range of property consulting services, from design to finding tenants and management, as hotel management companies do.

Explaining the new partnership, he said that when a property company is purely a leasing manager (asset-light), many similar managers spring up and undercut one another, and the market falls into disorder. "Only when you share in the asset's appreciation yourself (meaning the rise in property value after design and renovation) will you put your whole heart into creating it."

For investors, though, the point is clear: if the new model works, this renovation and leasing company will no longer depend mainly on slow, unsteady rental income, and more of its revenue can come from high management fees and rising property values. In January 2016, Yicheng Creative was listed on the NEEQ.

Image sources: Yicheng Creative, [Arting365](http://opus.arting365.com/entironment/2013-05-08/1367995450d270691.html), [ShanghaiWOW](http://www.shanghaiwow.com/2015/08/4282)
